stem.text: The continuous function \( f \) is defined on the closed interval \( -5 \le x \le 6 \) by \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2 & \text{for } -5 \le x \le 0 \\ 2 - x & \text{for } 0 < x \le 2 \\ -\sqrt{4 - (x - 4)^{2}} & \text{for } 2 < x \le 6 \end{cases} \] so the graph of \( f \) consists of two line segments and a semicircle below the \( x \)-axis. Let \( g \) be the function defined by \( g(x) = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{x} f(t)\,dt \) for \( -5 \le x \le 6 \).

worked_solution.text: On [-5, -2] f is below the axis in a triangle of base 3 and height 3; on [-2, 0] it is above in a triangle of base 2 and height 2.
Reversing the limits changes the sign.
A triangle of base 2 and height 2 above the axis on [0, 2], then a semicircle of radius 2 below the axis on [2, 6].

points.criterion: Gives g(-5) = 5/2, found from the two triangles on [-5, 0] with the sign reversed for the reversed limits. Any exact equivalent, or 2.5, is accepted.
Gives g(6) = 2 - 2pi, the triangle of area 2 plus the signed semicircle area -2pi. Any exact equivalent is accepted.

parts.prompt: Find \( g'(-3) \). Find the open intervals on which \( g \) is decreasing. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.answer_latex: g'(-3) = -1; \ g \text{ is decreasing on } (-5, -2) \text{ and } (2, 6)

worked_solution.text: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus g' = f.
Evaluate at x = -3 with the first piece.
g is decreasing where g' = f is negative.
worked_solution.latex: f(x) < 0 \text{ for } -5 < x < -2 \text{ and for } 2 < x < 6

points.criterion: Uses g'(x) = f(x), in general or at x = -3, and gives g'(-3) = f(-3) = -1. A value of -1 with no link to f does not earn the point.

Gives both intervals -5 < x < -2 and 2 < x < 6 (endpoints optional), with the reason that g'(x) = f(x) < 0 there. Only one of the two intervals, or no reason tied to the sign of f, does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Find the open intervals on which the graph of \( g \) is concave up and the open intervals on which it is concave down. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.answer_latex: \text{concave up on } (-5, 0) \text{ and } (4, 6); \text{ concave down on } (0, 4)

worked_solution.text: g'' = f', so the graph of g is concave up where f is increasing and concave down where f is decreasing.
f increases on the first segment and on the right half of the semicircle.
worked_solution.latex: f'(x) > 0 \text{ for } -5 < x < 0 \text{ and for } 4 < x < 6

worked_solution.text: f decreases on the second segment and on the left half of the semicircle.

points.criterion: Gives concave up on both -5 < x < 0 and 4 < x < 6 (endpoints optional), with the reason that g' = f is increasing there. One of the two intervals alone does not earn the point.

Gives concave down on 0 < x < 4 (endpoints optional), with the reason that g' = f is decreasing there. Using the intervals where f is negative instead of where f is decreasing does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Find the absolute maximum value of \( g \) on the closed interval \( -5 \le x \le 6 \). Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: Interior critical points of g are where g'(x) = f(x) = 0.
g at x = -2 reverses the triangle above the axis on [-2, 0].
g at x = 2 is the triangle on [0, 2].
Compare the candidates with the endpoint values from part (a).
The largest is at the left endpoint.

points.criterion: Sets g'(x) = f(x) = 0, or discusses where f changes sign, to identify the interior critical points x = -2 and x = 2.

Evaluates g at both interior critical points and both endpoints, g(-5) = 5/2, g(-2) = -2, g(2) = 2 and g(6) = 2 - 2pi, and compares them. Missing the endpoint x = -5, a wrong evaluation, or a local argument alone does not earn the point.
Gives the absolute maximum value 5/2, attained at x = -5. Any exact equivalent, or 2.5, is accepted.
